wordiness.question: (1) The committee reviewed each and every application before making a final decision. (2) Applicants were asked to submit a résumé, a cover letter, and two references. (3) The strongest candidates were invited back for a second round of interviews. (4) The committee announced its decision by email the following week. Which sentence should be revised to correct a wordiness issue?
wordiness.reasoning: (1) The committee reviewed each and every application before making a final decision. → The committee reviewed every application before making a final decision. "Each" and "every" mean the same thing here — pairing them doesn't add emphasis, it just says the same word twice. One or the other is enough.

wordiness.question: (1) The research team spent months collecting data before they began their final analysis. (2) Every single one of the participants completed the entire survey without skipping any questions. (3) The results revealed a clear connection between sleep quality and memory performance. (4) Researchers plan to publish their findings in a peer-reviewed journal next year. Which sentence should be revised to correct a wordiness issue?
wordiness.reasoning: (2) Every single one of the participants completed the entire survey... → All of the participants completed the entire survey... "Every," "single," and "one" are all doing the same job of emphasizing totality — stacking all three doesn't add meaning, it just repeats it. "All of the participants" or "Every participant" says the exact same thing in fewer words.

wordiness.question: (1) The weather service issued an advance warning before the storm made landfall, giving residents time to prepare. (2) Emergency shelters opened across the county to house anyone who needed a safe place to stay. (3) Volunteers distributed food, water, and blankets throughout the week. (4) Local officials praised the community's quick response to the crisis. Which sentence should be revised to correct a wordiness issue?
wordiness.reasoning: (1) The weather service issued an advance warning before the storm made landfall... → The weather service issued a warning before the storm made landfall... "Advance warning" is redundant — a warning is, by definition, something given in advance. It could simply say "a warning."

wordiness.question: (1) Due to the fact that ticket sales exceeded expectations, the concert venue added a second show. (2) Fans who missed out on the first round of tickets rushed to buy seats for the new date. (3) The band announced that proceeds from the extra show would support a local music education program. (4) Reviewers praised the added performance as even stronger than the first. Which sentence should be revised to correct a wordiness issue?
wordiness.reasoning: (1) Due to the fact that ticket sales exceeded expectations, the concert venue added a second show. → Because ticket sales exceeded expectations, the concert venue added a second show. "Due to the fact that" is a wordy way of saying "because" — it takes five words to do the job of one, without adding any meaning.
